# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Felix, Eleanor and Daniel all weigh what the yield is worth once the fee comes off. Irene and Jamal both say the bank already does the job. Ravi's board sign-off fits neither group, so leaving it on its own is right, and both names are plain words I'd use myself.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, idea, who pays, then how it sells, and the buyer questions sit where I'd expect: who decides before what it costs, and friction before the first step.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the identical heading and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so from the list alone the context step looks asked twice, though they may be two halves of one form.
founder.missing: A way to state my price as a share of the balance: Palus charges a flat 0.25% a year on assets under management, but screen 13 only takes an amount per period, so I had to pick a $4M-$6M reserve and turn it into $800-$1,200 a month. I also had no way to name the core advantage, more yield on the same cash; none of the advantage codes means 'more money'.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It runs naturally from what I'm leaving on the table, to what I'd pay, to who signs and how long diligence takes, and ends with whether I'd actually move money, though the counter jumps from 2 of 6 to 4 of 6, so a screen seems to be missing.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Where the reserve sits today and what I pay for it now (we pay Mercury's treasury fee, about $2,000 a month), how much cash we hold, and how fast I'd need to get it back; also nothing on safety of principal or custody (FDIC/SIPC, who holds the assets), which is the first thing my board would ask.

screens.why3: I know the gap between what Mercury or Brex Treasury pays and what a short-duration bond book earns on my own reserve, so I can state it as a share of the reserve a year.
screens.why4: Money, time and share are distinct and cover how this cost could be counted, and 'I'm not sure' is the right single escape for the founder's side.
screens.why5: My RATE, 2%, the long-term reserve, per company, a year and my loss line are all kept exactly, and the belief names venture-backed startups, not finance leads.
screens.why7: The rate is on the founder's base, unit and period, the heading's payer matches the belief's paying unit in the plural, the number is not redrawn, and the one escape is there.
screens.instead: What does this problem cost venture-backed startups today? A share they lose: 2% of the long-term reserve a year, the yield given up by leaving it in the bank's treasury · I'm not sure

screens.why1: Right after the cost question, asking what I'd charge is the obvious next step in 'will they pay', and the intro says plainly that 'No price yet' drops it.
screens.why2: 'A percent of the long-term reserve' and 'a fee per company each year' are how I and every treasury provider talk about pricing, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: My pricing is my own decision: a flat 0.25% annual fee on what the company puts with us, so I know the answer exactly.
screens.why4: The five shapes cover the ways treasury products charge, from a flat fee to a percent of balance, setup plus fee, one-off and free; they are distinct, my shape is there, and 'No price yet' is the right escape.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 0.25% a year and puts it on the long-term reserve, which is the money that comes to us, so it still means the fee I announced.
screens.why7: The percent is of money the payer holds and the base is named, my whole value, period and the idea's name are kept in the 'would think a fee of ... fair for Palus' form, and the escape is there and alone.

screens.why1: Right after I set the price, asking who besides me has to sign off on moving the reserve is the obvious next question about how Palus sells.
screens.why2: "Who has to agree before they can buy" is how I'd say it myself, and the hint says plainly that up to two short roles or "Nobody" are fine.
screens.why3: I know who has to agree before our long-term reserve moves off the bank's treasury product (the board, sometimes a lead investor), so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A free box capped at two roles of up to four words, with "Nobody" allowed and "I'm not sure" as the only chip, covers every answer I could give.
screens.why5: It names the startup founder as the one who decides, as I set on the who-decides screens, and takes "The board" in my own words.
screens.why7: The box matches the card's founder list: at most two roles, four words each, "Nobody" as an answer, and "I'm not sure" as the only founder-side escape, which leaves the dimension out.

screens.why1: Right after I named the board as the one who has to agree, it is obvious Keel would show me the list it built so I can check it before it becomes the belief.
screens.why2: Finance lead, startup founder, the board, has the problem, decides to buy and has to agree are all words I use with batchmates every week; only the intro repeating the title is a small stutter.
screens.why3: Who runs the cash, who signs where the reserve sits and whether the board must agree is exactly what I know from our own raise and from the founders I sell to.
screens.why4: Nobody else fixed first, then the finance lead with the problem, me as founder deciding, and the board having to agree, each tagged once with no role I never named and nothing missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my split, finance lead lives it and founder signs, and keeps 'The board' as I typed it, not turned into nobody else.
screens.why7: The rows meet the card's shape: Nobody else fixed first, one row per named role, each under 4 words with one plain tag, the board as the single has-to-agree role, so the belief can read 'The startup founder decides, and the board must agree first.'

screens.why1: Right after I named the board as the one who has to agree and checked Keel's rows, choosing which version of that belief to test is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Nobody else' and 'The board · has to agree' are the words I use for my own cap table and governance, so the choice reads on first pass.
screens.why3: Whether I decide on the reserve alone or need the board to sign off on the cash policy is my own decision and something I know firsthand.
screens.why4: The two rows are the two real beliefs I could hold: I decide alone, or the board must agree. They are distinct, use my words, and Keel added nothing and dropped nothing.
screens.why5: The board I typed is kept as typed, and the belief reads 'The startup founder decides, and the board must agree first.', which is exactly what I meant.
screens.why7: Nobody else is fixed first, then my one role tagged 'has to agree'. The tested belief names the board rather than collapsing it to nobody else. The bar counts 'sign off myself' and 'board would have to agree' as for, so it can hold or fail, which matches the card's good example.

screens.why1: After who decides, asking what the startup must clear before moving the reserve to Palus is the natural next step in how it sells.
screens.why2: Diligence, board approval and a tax adviser's sign-off are my trade's own words, and the hint says plainly what a step is and what to leave out.
screens.why3: I know from the thread exactly what slows a founder down: weeks of diligence on a new provider, the board's view of the cash policy, and the tax adviser.
screens.why4: The only chip is the I'm not sure escape, which fits a box I type into; nothing is missing or odd.
screens.why5: My three steps sit in the box exactly as I typed them, in my order, with nothing rewritten.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 buyer-side brakes of at most 9 words, biggest first, excludes my own trial or pilot, and promises the founder types the time next, all as the card requires, with I'm not sure as the founder's escape.

screens.why1: Right after I named what must clear before paying, Keel shows me the drafted steps to check, so it is obvious why this screen is here.
screens.why2: Board approval of the cash policy, diligence on a new provider and a tax adviser's sign-off are how founders and finance leads talk about moving a reserve, though 'purchase' is a slightly odd word for opening a treasury account.
screens.why3: These are the gates I have watched founders hit: boards and their investors on treasury policy, weeks of diligence, and the PHC and QSBS questions for the tax adviser.
screens.why4: Three distinct rows, none overlapping, each under 9 words with its object, and nothing silly or missing for this buyer.
screens.why5: All three rows come from my own material ('weeks to diligence', 'talk to their tax advisor', the board and NVCA treasury guidelines), and none of them is my pitch or my onboarding.
screens.why7: Every row is a brake on the buyer's own side that I do not control, there are 1 to 4 of them, none repeats another, none is the purchase itself or my offer, and the board's cash-policy approval plausibly leads as the biggest blocker.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the three steps my buyer's side must clear, picking one to test and saying how long it takes is the obvious next move in the will-they-pay section.
screens.why2: Board approval of the cash policy, diligence on a new provider, and a tax adviser's sign-off on the bonds are how a startup finance person talks, and 'how long would this one step take them' reads on the first pass.
screens.why3: I know from my own launch thread that founders say 'it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering', so a time in weeks is something I can actually estimate.
screens.why4: The three steps are distinct buyer-side brakes, none repeats another, and 'I'm not sure' is the right escape for the founder's own time.
screens.why5: The step I picked, 'Diligence on a new provider', and the 4 weeks I typed are carried unchanged into the belief and the bar.
screens.why7: Each row is a buyer-side step with its object, not my offer or pitch. The time is mine, typed in the box and not prefilled. The bar puts the edge at my 4 weeks, with 'under 4 weeks or not needed' counting for, so the belief can be both supported and refuted. The escape is present.

screens.why1: After price, who agrees and the purchase friction, asking what first step I'd want a founder to take is the obvious last piece of how Palus sells.
screens.why2: It asks two things at once, and 'what would it cost them' fits Palus badly: moving part of the reserve isn't a cost (the money stays theirs and earns), so I had to read the hint's 'where any money goes' to know I should name Palus rather than a fee.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I ask founders to do first, because I tell them to 'start small, try us out, and grow your position over time'.
screens.why4: The only option is the 'I'm not sure' chip, and it fits: a founder unsure of the first step can leave the dimension out.
screens.why5: My answer 'move a small part of the reserve into Palus' stands as typed: nine words, keeping 'a small part' and the product's name.
screens.why7: The card wants one founder step of at most nine words with 'I'm not sure' allowed, and this screen asks for exactly that, says where the money goes, and promises the smaller free step on the Check as the card requires.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the founder to take, and where would any money go? (one step, up to 9 words)

screens.why1: After I named my first step, this screen checks how strangers will hear it and adds the free step before it, which is the obvious place for it.
screens.why2: "Move a small part of the reserve into Palus" and "a demo on sample data" are plain to a founder holding cash from a raise; "the reserve" is how we talk about the long-term money.
screens.why3: A founder knows whether they would move part of their reserve, or would first want to see it work on sample data; it is their own call about their own cash.
screens.why4: The four answers are complete and distinct: a firm yes to the step, a soft yes after a free demo, probably not, and no, with no escape needed.
screens.why5: My step is kept whole: a small part, the reserve, and into Palus, which is my "start small, try us out". The sample-data demo is Keel's draft, but it is a fair zero-cost look before money moves.
screens.why7: The step is 9 words, in base form, and names what moves and where; it costs money, so a free smaller step is right, and the served list is right (for, for, against, against; no escape). But the smaller-step field holds "Yes, after a demo on sample data first" instead of the noun phrase the card asks for, which bends the smaller_step shape even though the served option reads correctly.
screens.instead: Keep the step and the list as served, but make the smaller-step field read just "a demo on sample data", so the served option stays "Probably, after a demo on sample data first".

screens.why1: Right before people see the study, deciding whether to ask for a real try of the step I just named (move a small part of the reserve into Palus) is the obvious last commercial choice.
screens.why2: Pilot, leave your email and the Pilot tab are plain to a startup founder, and the hint says exactly what strangers will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want early sign-ups from strangers is my own call, and I already tell people to start small and try us out.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole choice here, and the two options are distinct and complete.
screens.why5: My answer keeps the step I typed, but the line strangers see says 'try this for real' rather than naming the small first move into Palus, so my start-small framing drifts a little.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: 'Would you move a small part of your reserve into Palus to try it? Leave your email.' Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions belongs here, after the study is built and just before the link goes out to finance leads.
screens.why2: The hint says the interviewer asks 'on video' but then only asks me to pick a voice, so I have to reread to work out whether I'm also picking the face that finance leads will see.
screens.why3: Choosing which interviewer my own study uses, and spending my own credits on it, is my decision.
screens.why4: Two distinct, playable options with the default marked, and no escape is needed when I just keep the preselected one.
screens.why5: My answer was to keep the face Keel preselects, Daphne is preselected, and nothing here changes my idea or roles.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads your questions on video? Daphne is picked for you; tap Saskia to see and hear her and switch. 400 credits either way. (Daphne ▶ · Saskia ▶)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is natural to choose how the founders I'm sending Part 3 to will answer, before the link goes out.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but I am a founder myself, so "How should founders answer?" takes a second read to see it means the founders who get my link, not me.
screens.why3: I know how busy startup founders take a request: a short read-and-tap on a phone between meetings, rarely a video call with an AI.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choices: voice with Daphne, text, or let them pick; I picked "Read and tap" and it is there.
screens.why5: It keeps my decision-maker role, startup founders, and adds nothing about Palus that would leak to respondents.
screens.instead: How should the startup founders you send this to answer? (AI interviewer · Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose)

screens.why1: At the send step it is obvious I have to say who gets the study, and it comes right after choosing how founders answer.
screens.why2: The first two options are plain, but 'A group, with one open link' plus the Google sign-in detail takes a second read, and 'Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's screens.
screens.why3: I know who I would send this to: batchmates and finance leads I know by name, so it is answerable from my own life.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach finance leads, but 'found with Keel' and 'by name' overlap since both end in a link per person that I send myself.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my idea or roles; it only asks about distribution.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I already know (one link each) / A list from Keel's Contacts search (one link each) / One open link I post where finance leads gather, like a YC batch Slack

screens.why_b1: The verdict Not holding up sits beside its number (1 of 7 lose 2% or more), but the page says the verdict is the worst card, and two cards say Did not hold, which reads as worse, so the deciding number and the verdict do not clearly line up.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives a count over n with a bar (1 of 7, bar 5 of 7), but Not holding up and Did not hold sit side by side with no stated difference, and the kicker 1 TO 8 COUNTED takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are mine and the 2% and 0.25% lines follow my numbers, but I said the founder decides with nobody else, and the card says the board must agree first.
screens.why_b4: The status lines (they lose less than you estimated, they value it below your price) are generic, and nothing says what to change, such as framing the cost as yield given up on a $5M reserve or showing a smaller first commitment.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible and Ability to pay is marked too few to call, but 1 TO 8 COUNTED is garbled, and the verdict names one Not holding up card while two Did not hold cards look worse.
screens.instead: Did not hold: founders report losing far less than 2% a year (1 of 7), only 1 of 8 call 0.25% fair, and 4 of 8 would move a small part, so test whether founders count yield given up as a cost before testing price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Not holding up, sits right beside the deciding number: 1 of 7 at 2% or more against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: It is plain that the chart counts the percent of the long-term reserve a year for 7 people, but there are two bars: my 2% on the 0-3 axis and a bar marker at 5 on a strip of 7 people, so it takes a second look to see which is which.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice and about 2% of the long-term reserve a year, as yield given up by leaving it at the bank, is the belief I typed.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and points me to the Price card, but it doesn't say what this means for my pitch, for instance that founders don't feel foregone yield as a cost, so a pitch about money they're losing won't land.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible and says a lean, not a call, but the headline 'they lose less today than you estimated' reads as fact, when people asked what they 'went without' may simply not count yield they never saw.
screens.instead: 1 of 7 say they gave up 2% or more of the reserve last year, and most named little or none (a small group, a lean). Founders may not count yield they never received as a cost, so lead with the extra dollars Palus earns, not with what the bank costs them.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside 1 of 8 at 0.25% or more against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know the belief failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bands, each band's count, my 0.25% marked as the low edge of its band, and the strip with the marker at 6 of 8 all read on the first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief, a fee of 0.25% of the long-term reserve a year, is my flat 0.25% on AUM in my own terms, said of the founders who decide.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me most chose 0.1% to under 0.25%, but it stops there and sends me to Insights instead of saying what to change, such as testing a fee below 0.25% against what the bank's treasury already charges.
screens.why_b5: n is shown, all 8 are counted, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said, and nothing claims more than 1 of 8; the quotes that speak of a fee "every month" or "a few hundred a month" are a little loose but do not mislead.
screens.instead: Fewer than 2 in 3 would pay 0.25%; most picked 0.1% to under 0.25%, so test a fee nearer what their bank's treasury charges, or show the yield after fees, before keeping 0.25%.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know nothing is decided and why.
screens.why_b2: The strip is plain: 1 cell for me, 4 empty, the bar at 4 of 5. The chart above it is a bare 0 to 2.5 scale with no label, so I have to look twice to see it counts people.
screens.why_b3: I can recognise the 0.25% fee and the long-term reserve, but 'paid out of the gain' is Keel's derived reading, not a line I checked. The Asked line is the where-would-the-money-come-from question, which doesn't match a belief judged on what people lose.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' is a generic wait. It doesn't tell me that 7 of 8 founders stopped below my price, so the real problem is Price, not where the money comes from.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said ('a lean, not a call'), but Maya Feldman is marked 'loses your price or more' next to her Price band, 0.25% to under 0.5%. That reads her price as her loss, and the So line says she 'said where the money would come from', so the card mixes two readings.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Maya named 0.25% or more, and 7 of 8 stopped below it, so fix the price before this can be asked. Show what Maya loses today, not her price band, and drop the budget question from a card read on loss.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 8 as you said or easier against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know at once that it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over all 8 founders, each marked for or against. The strip shows 7 for, 1 against, with the marker at 6, so what is counted, out of how many and where the bar sits are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'The startup founder decides, and the board must agree first' are my belief as I set it, with the board I typed named in both the belief and the question.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the board in most deals' gets the result backwards: only 2 of 8 said the board would have to agree and 5 of 8 could sign alone, so the next step it gives me is wrong.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n visible and says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the So line's 'most deals' claims a board role the 8 answers do not carry, and it never says that fewer had to agree than I said.
screens.instead: Holding up, and fewer had to agree than you said: 5 of 8 could sign alone, 2 needed the board and 1 needed several people, so pitch the founder directly and keep board material ready for the minority who need it; a small group, a lean, not a call.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside the deciding count, 3 of 8 under 4 weeks or not needed against a bar of 6 of 8, 3 short, so I know the answer and the number behind it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts how long the diligence would take, band by band, over 8 founders, and the strip shows 3 for and 5 against with the marker at 6, so I see at once how far short it falls.
screens.why_b3: The step is the one I picked, diligence on a new provider, and the time is the 4 weeks I typed, so the belief line is mine; the line labelled as the bar only repeats the step, which is a little odd.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely to plan for a sales cycle of 4 weeks to 3 months rather than my five-minute pitch, and points me to the Insights tab for what eats the time.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly calls 8 a lean, not a call, but the flat "Did not hold" is firmer than the "Not holding up" my other cards used at the same n, and "longer than your 4 weeks" counts people whose band starts at exactly 4 weeks.
screens.instead: Not holding up: 5 of 8 founders put diligence at 4 weeks to 3 months (a band that starts at your 4 weeks), only 3 within it or not needing it, a lean from 8, so plan for a one-to-three-month cycle and find what takes the time on Insights.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "4 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 2 short", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts my eight founders' answers to the one step. It shows 4 firm yeses, 0 soft and 2 + 2 against, and the strip puts the marker at 6 of 8 with the 1-in-3 rule spelled out, so all three things read at once.
screens.why_b3: "Move a small part of the reserve into Palus", decided by the startup founder, is my commitment step word for word, though "You said move a small part..." reads clumsily and "if it were offered today" repeats "If it were ready today".
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the 4 who would not and sends me to the Insights tab. It doesn't tell me what the split means: half say a firm yes with no soft middle, and the four against are firm too, so a demo-first offer is unlikely to win them and the question is whether a smaller trial or board-ready diligence would.
screens.why_b5: "Did not hold" is stated flatly while the count line calls 8 "a lean, not a call", which is a mild contradiction. "What they would start with instead" also assumes the two firm Nos would start with something at all.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean on 8: 4 founders would move a small part of the reserve into Palus now and none wanted a demo first; the 4 against were firm (2 No, 2 probably not), so look at what stops them, like board sign-off, diligence or tax, before betting on a smaller trial.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Not holding up, Did not hold) with the deciding count and bar beside it: 1 of 8 against a bar of 6, 3 of 8 with 3 short, and 4 of 8 with 2 short.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment are my dimensions, and the belief lines carry my own terms: 0.25% of the long-term reserve, diligence on a new provider within about 4 weeks, and a small part of the reserve into Palus.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these results mean for Palus; it shows quotes and counts, and the Purchase friction and Commitment boxes are empty question headers with nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: The count lines add up and name who never saw each question, nothing is called strong, and the empty boxes say 0 asked here rather than inventing a reason.
screens.why_b6: The Price quotes teach me something I had not typed: founders weigh the fee against the one-point spread, not the balance; they would look at something closer to the bank's own fee; and the board's comfort with mortgage bonds, not diligence time, is what gates the move.
screens.instead: Say plainly that founders read 0.25% as a cut of a one-point gain, so price on the spread or near the bank's fee, and either pull Felix's paper trial and Ravi's two board calls into the Commitment and Purchase friction boxes or say there that their reasons were given on Price.

screens.why1: The kicker says this is the buying decision, so it makes sense to show me what I'd be deciding on before asking whether I'd move cash into it.
screens.why2: Treasury account, custodian and money market fund are my words, but 'short-duration, floating-rate' needs a second read, and I'd say 'cash we won't touch for a year' rather than 'long-term reserve'.
screens.why3: Where our raise sits and what it earns versus Mercury's money market sweep is exactly what I decide.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It reads as one coherent pitch, a higher-yield government-backed bond account for idle startup cash, with nothing beyond the idea itself leaking.
screens.why6: Heard once, the 'how it works' runs five sentences instead of one line, and 'short-duration, floating-rate and government-backed' plus 'treasury account' said twice is a mouthful to hold before '4.5 to 5 percent' lands.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account that puts the cash you won't need for a year into government-backed mortgage bonds. It links to your bank, a regulated custodian holds the bonds in your company's name, and cash reaches checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent, against about 3.5 percent after fees in your bank's money market fund.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, opening the buying part by asking what the current setup already costs me is the obvious place for it.
screens.why2: "What percent of the long-term reserve did you go without" reads like I spent or lost part of my reserve, and it never says it means the interest I didn't earn, so I'd have to guess what's being asked.
screens.why3: I know roughly what our cash earned and what treasuries paid, so I could work out the yield gap as a percent of the reserve, but I'd be estimating rather than recalling a number I track.
screens.why4: A percent box, None as zero and one I-can't-recall escape cover every true answer without overlap.
screens.why5: The base and period look kept, but "go without" drops the founder's actual loss, the interest on cash sitting in the operating account, so the meaning has drifted.
screens.why6: It's short and has one escape, but heard once, "what percent of the long-term reserve did you go without" is ambiguous and the label echo "a percent of the long-term reserve last year" adds nothing.
screens.why7: The measure, base and period match the founder's (a percent of the reserve a year), so it can support or refute the belief, but the item uses the vague "go without" the card warns against and never names the interest it is losing.
screens.instead: Last year, about what percent of the long-term reserve did you not earn in interest because it sat in your operating account? [ box ] % of the reserve last year · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what I'd pay is the obvious next thing, and I'm the one who signs off on where our raise sits and what we pay for it.
screens.why2: A percent a year on held cash is how I already think about treasury fees, but 'long-term reserve' isn't what I call it; to me it's our runway or the cash from the raise, and I had to stop and work out which money they meant.
screens.why3: I already pay our bank's treasury fee, about $2,000 a month, and I know what yield we get, so I can say what fee on that cash would feel fair.
screens.why4: The bands run cleanly from under a tenth of a percent to a percent or more, with no overlap; 'I wouldn't pay for this' covers a real answer and 'I can't say' sits apart.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but 'the long-term reserve' reads like the product's own word for our cash, not mine, so the meaning drifted a little from how a founder would put it.
screens.why6: Spoken in two short steps, with the percents said as a quarter and half a percent and one escape said last, it's easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: It is a percent of money I hold, with six rungs, 'to under' on every band and 'or more' on the last, then 'I wouldn't pay' and the 'I can't say' escape apart; there are bands both below and above a quarter-percent edge, so the belief can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: Palus takes a yearly fee on the cash it holds for you. What fee a year would feel fair to you? Under 0.1% · 0.1% to under 0.25% · 0.25% to under 0.5% · 0.5% to under 1% · 1% or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I named a fee, asking what would make Palus worth more is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: It reads my own pick back as I'd say it, a tenth to a quarter of a percent a year, and 'worth more' is plain to me.
screens.why3: I know what I'd want from a treasury product (same-day liquidity, insured or T-bill backing, a better yield than Mercury's sweep), so I can answer from my own needs.
screens.why4: A free-text box with no options.
screens.why5: Palus and its yearly fee came from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing new about the founder's plan reaches me here.
screens.why6: Spoken as figures, 'zero point one percent to zero point two five percent' is a mouthful; it should be said in words, 'a tenth to a quarter of a percent a year', as the guidelines ask.
screens.instead: You said about a tenth to a quarter of a percent a year for Palus. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: Right after I named a fee, asking whether I can sign off on it myself or need the board is the obvious next step for where our raise money sits.
screens.why2: Sign off and the board are everyday words for a founder-CEO, and I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether moving treasury money needs board approval at my company, because I'm the one who'd have to ask them.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone, to the board, to several people, to not my call, each opening differently, and I can't say fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The board is a role any founder already lives with, so nothing about Palus's plan or the founder's own terms leaks through.
screens.why6: It's one short either-or question, then four short options as a list I can hold, and the escape said last.
screens.why7: The four options, their order, the board named in the second, and the escape all match the card, but the stem says sign off on Palus rather than on the price the card asks for (about 0.25% of the balance a year), so the measure is a little looser than it should be.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about 0.25% of the balance a year yourself, or would the board have to agree? I could sign off myself · The board would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether the board would have to agree, asking how long checking out a new place for our cash would take is the obvious next step in the buying story.
screens.why2: Diligence is a word I live with as a founder, and checking out a new provider before moving raise money is exactly how I'd put it.
screens.why3: I've moved cash between Mercury, a sweep account and T-bills, so I know roughly how long my own checks on a provider, and my board's, would take.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and don't overlap, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a real answer for a small company that would just do it, and 'I can't tell' fits a purchase I haven't made.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch leaks here; the step reads as my own side's check on a new provider, in words I'd use.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short, and the four-then-two split (under 4 weeks, 4 weeks to 3 months, over 3 months, or not needed, then the band within) is easy to hold.
screens.why7: The step is a brake on the buyer's side with one band edge at 4 weeks; three answers count for (under 2 weeks, 2 to under 4 weeks, not needed) and three against (4 weeks and up), and the single 'I can't tell' escape is set apart.

screens.why1: After fee, sign-off and diligence, the last thing to ask is whether I'd actually put money in, so this is the natural close of the buying questions.
screens.why2: Moving a small part of the reserve into a new account is exactly how I'd think about trying a treasury provider, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I'm the one who decides where the raise sits, so whether I'd move a slice of it is a call I'd really make.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and complete, but 'a demo on sample data' reads like a software trial; for a bond-backed account I'd want a call with the team or a look at the actual holdings, not sample data.
screens.why5: Palus and the reserve come from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and 'a small part' keeps the founder's limited step without adding urgency or numbers.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four answers I can hold, and the first option is long but still easy to say.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's own step whole, the soft yes is a free smaller step and not the step again, there are two answers for and two against, and there's no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you move a small part of the reserve into Palus, or not? · Yes, I'd move a small part of the reserve into Palus · Probably, after a call to see the holdings first · Probably not · No
